paragraphs: Since Wang Meng’s death, the lamps in the Department of State Affairs had scarcely gone out.

Before dawn in Chang’an, couriers from the provinces were already waiting beneath the galleries. Some carried military registers, others accounts of grain and taxes. A great bamboo basket beside the door was reserved for urgent dispatches, and within an hour its bottom had disappeared from view. Fu Hong had spent his days here copying accounts and reading memorials. He had watched officials argue an entire morning over two measures of grain, and seen an apparently ordinary transfer order take laborers from the spring fields of three counties in Hedong. Gradually he understood why the entire court had feared Wang Meng while he lived. It was not that his voice had thundered over the hall. He remembered, behind every fine-sounding pronouncement, the people who would have to carry out the bitter and petty work.
Today would be different. Fu Jian had ordered him to preside over the discussion alone and decide how the First Battalion of the new army would be established.

The crown prince reached the main hall before the morning hour of mao. Quan Yi came to meet him carrying a faded outer robe, its sleeve spotted with ink. Fu Hong asked whether he had gone home the previous night. “I did. Everyone was asleep when I arrived, and everyone was still asleep when I left.”
“Did Lord Wang work this hard?”
“Lord Wang was always telling me I was too slow.” Quan Yi smiled and placed a stack of military registers before the prince. “Now that he is gone, I find myself wishing someone would say it again.”

Wang Meng’s old desk still stood at the far end of the hall. Its corners had been worn pale, and two broken brushes remained in the holder. Fu Hong did not sit there. He arranged a place for himself to one side and asked for three piles of memorials. The first came from Di princes and veteran generals; the second from Han Chinese ministers proposing changes to command, rations, and law; the third from the Qiang, the Xianbei, and soldiers surrendered from other peoples. Quan Yi observed that if fewer than thirty memorials arrived on any given day, something must have happened on the postal roads.

Fu Hong began with those from the imperial clan. Several were written in ringing tones, recalling the family’s founding struggles and the blood shed by fathers and brothers. To strip them of their old soldiers, they argued, was to forget the men who had built Qin. Only one letter was written plainly. It came from Fu Chong’s residence: “Our old soldiers are leaving the camps, yet the families of those killed in battle still come to my household for relief. Now that the troops and the households have been separated, from whom are they to claim the two years of payments still owing?”
Fu Hong drew that letter out and placed it at the corner of his desk.

Pei Xuan’s memorial was the neatest of the Han ministers'. He described the old military arrangements: troops of different peoples did not yet obey the same commands or wear the same colors; if they were forced together by decree, the camp might erupt before an enemy appeared. Only at the end did he add that the army must not be reorganized in haste merely because of words spoken by Wang Meng on his deathbed. Quan Yi told Fu Hong that the Pei family had dependent military households in Hedong, so they too had interests at stake in any redistribution of the old armies.
“Does that make him wrong?” Fu Hong asked.
“Which part?”
“That the commands are not yet uniform, and hasty mixing would bring disorder.”
“On that he is right.”
“Then why bring Lord Wang into it?”
“To make people angry before they listen.” Quan Yi turned to another page. “Once you are angry with him, you may throw away the truth in the earlier sentence along with the provocation at the end.”
Fu Hong said nothing. He put Pei Xuan’s memorial beside the first letter.

Among the third pile was a petition from a Xianbei commandant whose handwriting wandered across the page. He had obeyed Qin’s orders to suppress bandits in Hedong and taken an arrow through his right shoulder. Yet the Di soldiers sharing his camp would not let him draw medicine there; he had been told to report back to his former unit. A Qiang archery detachment wrote that their orders had always been relayed through minor tribal commanders. If the army now issued commands in written Chinese, who could read the characters before an enemy struck at night? A surrendered Xiongnu general had even less to say: if everyone was to serve in one army, why did the Di always choose the offices before anyone else’s merit was considered?

Resentment colored every letter, yet each contained something true. Fu Hong read until sunrise, then spread the three piles across the desk. He had meant to select the soundest proposal among them. Instead he found that to grant what one side demanded was almost always to give another side fresh cause for grievance.

Quan Yi had a clerk bring the report that had arrived from Ye the previous night. The Prince of Yangping had removed the barriers separating people by ancestry. In a mutual-aid register kept by former Yan families, he had found entries added in a different hand. The source of the missing weapons remained unknown. The investigation continued, and no principal culprit could yet be named.

Holding the thin sheet, Fu Hong remembered the ministers surrendering their command tallies in Chongde Hall a few days earlier. His father had supposed that once deprived of their private armies, the chiefs would sit down and reason together. They had sat down, certainly, but each still gripped something else: past service, a set of accounts, the memory of an insult.

In the afternoon the ministers assembled. Fu Chong sent word that he was ill and did not attend. The imperial clan was represented by his younger kinsman Fu Mo, who was not yet old but already possessed the pride of an ancient house. He brought a leather case crammed with records of Fu family campaigns since Qin’s founding. The Xianbei commanders chose Murong Shao to speak; the Qiang sent two company leaders and a registrar who could write Chinese. Pei Xuan sat at the head of the civil officials with a closely written agenda in his lap.

Fu Hong had prepared an opening address. But as the men took their seats, he felt that to deliver those polished sentences would be like negotiating with them from behind a closed door. He slipped the draft beneath his papers.
“Today we shall not argue about the old kingdoms or our ancestors,” he began. “We shall decide whose grain the First Battalion eats, whose orders it obeys, and who judges a soldier who disobeys.”

Fu Mo rose at once. “We must first decide who is fit to command. The Fu family carved the realm of Great Qin out of a mountain of corpses. How can its men be placed on the same footing as generals who surrendered from the fallen Yan?”
Murong Shao was already on his feet. “I held off two rebellions in Hebei for Qin and bear three arrow wounds. Did I receive those arrows fighting for Yan?”
“You may be willing to fight for Qin,” Fu Mo said, “but will you die for it?”
“Then take the field with me and see who dies first!”
“Do you mean to draw a sword here?”

Men rose from their mats on every side; even the Qiang delegates began pounding the tables. Twice Fu Hong asked them to sit, but his voice was swallowed by the uproar. He stared at the empty space in the middle of the hall. It was no more than a few paces wide, yet harder to hold than the thirty thousand names he had read the day before. The herald behind him dared not move: to summon the palace guards without orders might only make matters worse.
Then a voice came from the entrance. “The crown prince has asked you to be seated. Has no one heard him?”

Fu Jian stood beside the curtain in everyday robes, without a ceremonial escort and with only two attendants behind him. Everyone hurried to bow; the noise ceased at once. Fu Jian did not ascend to the presiding seat. He had a mat placed beside a pillar and motioned for Fu Hong to continue.
Heat rose into Fu Hong’s face. He had not won that moment of silence for himself. He picked up his brush, but did not retrieve the prepared address.

“Fu Mo,” he said first, “you wish to rank the troops by ancestral merit. Suppose half the cavalry in our new battalion once served Yan. When their commander meets the enemy, must he settle their genealogies before giving an order?”
“I am speaking of rightful precedence.”

“Past service is recorded; rank and reward are governed by law. We may consider the founders' merits separately. But among these thirty thousand men, may the punishment for cowardice be reduced because the coward bears the name Fu?”
Fu Mo set his jaw. “No.”
Fu Hong turned to Murong Shao. “You say the Di do not trust Yan soldiers. Would they trust you if the whole new battalion were entrusted to Xianbei officers?”
“Officers should be chosen for military merit.”
“Who verifies that merit?”
“The court.”
“Most court clerks come from Guanzhong. Do you trust them to do it?”
Murong Shao faltered, then sat slowly down.

The Qiang registrar seized the opening to speak of a night battle years before. The courier had died in a mountain pass; the rear ranks heard Han Chinese troops shouting and thought the order was to retreat. A cavalry unit charged straight through its own archers, trampling seventeen men to death. They could learn Chinese characters, he said, but a man’s life would not wait until his lessons were complete. Pei Xuan replied that the army had long employed banners and drums: unify the signals first and the registers afterward. Murong Shao argued that if every people understood the drums differently, the quarrel would merely begin again. This time there were no shouted insults, only the turning of paper. Fu Hong had the points in dispute written on wooden boards. When the list was finished it contained seventeen matters, not one of which could be settled by a single line of imperial decree.
“Six months,” Fu Hong said suddenly.
The ministers turned toward him.

“We will establish the First Battalion near the capital on a trial basis for six months. Verification of names and grain allocations begins today. The camp structure, flags and drums, and the cooperation of officers and men will be tested one matter at a time. For anything that does not work, write down why; no empty excuses. We will review troop movements and ration orders after three months, and consider extending the system to the provinces after six.”
He saw Fu Jian turn his head slightly, but the emperor said nothing.
Fu Mo was first to ask, “So the other old armies will remain untouched for six months?”
“They must surrender their registers as ordered. No one may transfer soldiers or their households privately. Full integration will begin with the First Battalion.”

Pei Xuan asked who would draft the regulations. Fu Hong called for officers from the central army, the Department of State Affairs, and the Court of Judicial Review, so that no single office controlled the work. Murong Shao demanded that former Yan officers take part in verifying service records. Fu Hong agreed, but required Di and Qiang representatives to inspect them together. The grain issued to a soldier must be supported by records anyone authorized could examine. Claims to military merit had to be filed and preserved for later checking, regardless of who submitted them first.
“And if an officer disobeys?” the Qiang registrar asked.
“He will be dealt with under the battalion’s regulations.”
“Even if he belongs to the Fu imperial clan?”
Fu Hong saw that Fu Mo had lifted his face to watch him. “Even then.”

Some ministers were satisfied; others were not. Fu Mo was relieved that the old armies would not be dismantled all at once and still hoped the decision might be altered. Pei Xuan was pleased that a night’s fervor would not replace the slow work of military administration. Murong Shao was already preparing to fight over the list of officers. Fu Hong saw the calculations behind their faces and felt a small measure of relief. No sword had been drawn, and the First Battalion finally had a date on which it would begin.
When the meeting ended, only father and son remained in the main hall. Quan Yi dismissed the clerks and closed the courtyard gate himself.
“Who taught you to say six months?” Fu Jian asked.
“No one. I thought of it myself.”
“When you said it, they all relaxed. Were you pleased?”
Fu Hong did not deny it.

Fu Jian picked up the old records Fu Mo had left behind and opened to a page with a torn corner. It recorded a campaign in Hedong: eight hundred cavalry sent out, one hundred ninety-six killed. In a line of smaller, paler characters someone had added, “Thirty-two missing.” Fu Jian pointed at it. “Should the old service be remembered?”
“Yes.”
“And the families of the dead, who have yet to receive their relief payments—should that be investigated?”
“Yes.”
“Suppose you find that a grain official of the Fu clan pocketed those payments?”
Fu Hong did not answer immediately. Fu Jian went on. “Or that a veteran Xianbei officer brought here by Murong Shao claimed another man’s merit?”
“He too must answer under the law.”

“Good.” Fu Jian closed the register. “In six months they will ask what your inspections found. Today you promised them a trial. You did not make them promise that they would accept the findings when punishment falls.”
Fu Hong looked uncomfortable. “I did say the military law would apply.”
“That is easy to say. It will be harder when you prosecute the first member of the imperial clan. Harder again when an old Yan general asks mercy on account of his wounds.”

Fu Hong pressed his lips together. After a long silence he said, “Was it easy for Father to take their tiger tallies last night? But you had the feathered guards behind you and the armies of the realm in your hands. If I had ordered those men to be quiet today, they would have obeyed only because you were here. Once you leave, who will listen to me?”

Fu Jian’s expression changed. What his son had endured that day was precisely the humiliation he had not wished to spare him. If the emperor intervened in every dispute, the crown prince would become no more than the shadow cast by an imperial seal.
“Do you think I should not have entered?” he asked.
“At the time I wanted you to come in,” Fu Hong said softly. “Now I wish you had stayed away.”
Fu Jian gave a brief laugh, then checked himself. After a moment he said, “Next time, if no one has drawn a sword, I shall stay outside.”

For a while they stood beside the old desk. Dusk gathered beyond the windows. White mourning streamers in the courtyard of the Department of State Affairs fluttered against the panes, their shadows moving lightly. Fu Hong suddenly asked, “What will Father do about those people in Ye?”
“The Prince of Yangping is still investigating.”
“Yet here in Chang’an everyone already calls them rebels.”
Fu Jian looked at his son. “Can you vouch for them?”
“No. I do not know them.”
“Then why speak for them?”

“Because if we arrest people merely for being unknown to us, something is wrong. If there must be someone to vouch for them, could the government not vouch that it has investigated its own case properly?”

Fu Jian sat down slowly. He remembered Wang Meng’s dying warning not to trust men too readily; he remembered the old widow’s straw sandals and the tiger tally Murong Chui had surrendered in Chongde Hall. Since Wang Meng’s death, he had sometimes feared that the smallest concession would let the empire split along its hidden seams. But listening to his son now, he feared something else still more: if the laws devised to prevent rebellion became the first thing that frightened people trying to survive, what could a million soldiers preserve?

“If the government is to vouch for its judgments, words alone will not do,” he said. “The joint verification you proposed for the First Battalion is a sound beginning. But some matters cannot be endlessly bargained away.”

Fu Jian tapped the desk with the back of his fingers. “Military registers belong to the court. Rations are to be issued by verified rolls. Service is not to be ranked by ancestry. No commander may keep an entire old army as his private following. These things are not favors to be traded. The rest—where to pitch the camp, which languages to use in giving orders, how to choose company leaders—may be tried and changed if they fail.”
Fu Hong thought a moment. “One thing is missing.”
“What?”
“The people who verify the accounts.”

He pushed the three piles of memorials nearer his father and pointed to one. “If we send only Guanzhong clerks to check Xianbei registers, they will call every duplicate name an accusation. If Xianbei officers check their own old troops, they will turn one man into two. I want men from different units to check one another, while the Court of Judicial Review and the ration office each keep a copy.”
Fu Jian did not praise him immediately. “What if they collude against you?”
“Then there must be another set of accounts to consult.”
“The inspectors can be bribed too.”
“I know,” Fu Hong said, holding his father’s gaze. “But if anyone can be bribed, that cannot mean only one man should ever hold the money.”

Fu Jian studied him, then nodded at last. He had Quan Yi bring out the draft roll prepared by the central army and placed it before his son. Murong Chui was named commanding general, Fu Chong his deputy. Thirty thousand troops were listed under their existing Di, Xianbei, Qiang, Han Chinese, and other divisions, to be counted anew once they reached the camp.
Fu Hong stared at the deputy’s name. “Fu Chong and Murong Chui in the same command tent?”
“If they will train only with men they already know, the court will have to arrange their friendships for them before every battle.”
“Fu Chong may refuse orders.”
“Then go and see whether he does.”
“I, Father?”

“I entrust you with verifying the military rolls. Within ten days, submit an actual register from which rations can be issued. I do not care how many men it shows. Record the errors and omissions. If you cannot produce the register, say so truthfully. Do not invent numbers to please me.”

Fu Hong opened the draft. The figures on the first page were exquisitely neat, adding up to exactly thirty thousand. After his days in the Department of State Affairs, he had learned to distrust numbers that came out quite so perfectly.
“What if three thousand are missing?”
“Then three thousand are missing.”
“The officers will say I have ruined morale.”
“Let them say it.” Fu Jian rose from behind the desk. “Better they curse you now than discover on the battlefield that those three thousand men never existed.”

Fu Jian left without turning back to give any further instruction. Standing at the desk, Fu Hong understood that this was different from the accounts he had copied in previous days. A mistaken line could be scraped clean and written again. The names he must now verify belonged to men riding along the frontiers, men buried ten years before, and men still drawing rations while spending every day laboring in a general’s fields. If he counted too many, the treasury would issue grain to ghosts. If he counted too few, living soldiers would go hungry. Every stroke of the brush could wound someone.

Quan Yi returned from the gallery and opened three sample rolls. The first, for Di troops, recorded 3,217 men, of whom 2,694 had actually appeared. The second, for a former Xianbei unit, included duplicate names in Ye and Hedong. The third, for Han Chinese troops, was beautifully complete: even the signatures of dead soldiers receiving rations had never changed. Quan Yi tapped that last roll with one finger. Such “perfect” records, he said, were harder to verify than either of the others.
“Did Lord Wang count every man himself?” Fu Hong asked.
“He did.”
“And afterward?”
“Some said he was cruel to wounded soldiers. Some sent villagers to impersonate enlisted men. One group carried the memorial tablets of the dead to the gates of his residence.”
“How did he respond?”
“He endured their abuse and kept counting. He made mistakes too. When he did, he repaid grain and offered apologies. Then he counted again.”

Fu Hong looked toward the empty desk. In everyone’s stories Wang Meng had seemed nearly infallible. Yet when Quan Yi spoke of him, he was a man who could misjudge and overlook things, a man obliged to answer to living people who would not arrange themselves neatly in an account book. The discovery eased Fu Hong’s mind. He need not imitate a dead man who had never erred; he had to learn the courage to reopen the ledger after a mistake.

That night, after the others had gone, Fu Hong divided the registrars for the new army into three groups: civilian clerks to compare old lists, military officers to identify the men, and ration officials to check actual distributions. He also asked the Court of Judicial Review to record disputed findings. Every people must be represented, but none might control an entire roll. At the foot of the sheet he added four questions he had not found time to put that afternoon: who would take over unpaid relief to families of the dead; how would a missing soldier be restored to the rolls if he returned; how could orders be carried when interpreters were scarce; and how would false and duplicate ration claims be recovered?
Late at night, Quan Yi came to ask whether a carriage should be brought to take him back to the palace. Fu Hong set down his brush and stretched his stiff fingers.
“I shall not come here tomorrow.”
“Does Your Highness have other business?”
“I am going to Xiliu Plain.”
“The soldiers have not all arrived. The camp itself is scarcely established.”

“So much the better. The tents are not yet up, and they have probably not learned to eat from the same pot. If I sit here waiting for a finished list, I shall only be staring at thirty thousand men on paper again.”

Quan Yi began to arrange the ceremonial escort of the Eastern Palace, but Fu Hong stopped him. He wanted only four guards and ten young clerks. Each was to carry a blank register, a brush, and a length of cord fine enough to hang at his waist. They would write names on the spot and check them there. Quan Yi asked whether senior officials should accompany the party.

“Today I have spent the whole day listening to men recount their ancestors' merits,” Fu Hong said. “Tomorrow I want to meet the men who are alive. If some cannot even write their own names, the more great officials we bring, the less likely they are to speak.”

When he left the Department of State Affairs, white mourning streamers still hung from Chang’an’s palace walls. At the steps he saw a squad of feathered guards changing watch. On one side the men wore the old short swords of the Di, on the other Xianbei leather pouches. The change-of-watch drum sounded, but they stepped aside for one another, neither willing to pass through the same narrow way first.

Fu Hong nearly went to speak with them, then swallowed the words. Instead he turned to his attendants and ordered them to bring measuring cords and the registers first thing in the morning, along with food. Why food, someone asked. The clerks would be walking all day, the prince answered, and would need to eat. If the camp really lacked grain, they might also learn how many men could share a day’s ration of cakes.

At dawn the next day, the vermilion-wheeled carriage of the Eastern Palace remained in its gallery. Fu Hong rode out in a plain blue robe, followed by barely a dozen horsemen, blank ledgers hanging from their saddles. Thick morning mist covered Xiliu Plain. Even from a distance he could hear men shouting over water inside the camp. Rows of wooden palisades reached into the white air; beyond them old banners had been raised, their differently colored ends twisting in the wind, like the banners of an army that had not yet decided what it should be called.

Fu Hong handed a blank military register to the clerk behind him and urged his horse toward the gate. Out of the mist a sentry raised his spear across the road. The prince caught his guard’s arm before the man could shout, and reined in his horse.
